subject: Hierarchical approach: estimating manifest variables from trial level data

messages.author: 24b2718934f39ab1
messages.subject: Hierarchical approach: estimating manifest variables from trial level data
parts:
Hi Ed and All,

My apologies if this question has been discussed elsewhere, here in this group (I am new) or in the reference documentation for blavaan. 

I have a bifactor latent change SEM that runs in both lavaan and blavaan. The manifest variables are based on average scores (mean performance), but I would like to go full hierarchical bayesian and estimate the manifest variables from trial-level data to take advantage of shrinkage.

Is this possible with blavaan? and if yes, can someone point me in the right direction?

Thank you,

Jean-Paul

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical approach: estimating manifest variables from trial level data
parts:
Hi Mauricio,

thanks for responding. As a cognitive psychologist I often work with behavioral experiments. 
These experiment have, let's say 100 trials, and for each of those I have an accuracy (0 or 1) and a reaction time. 
Where as a small subset of survey items are used as the manifest variables, for behavioral experiment it is common to take the mean accuracy or reaction time performance.
In this example pCE, pNE, and pSE are 3 separate experiments with each 100 trials, but we pass (b)lavaan the mean accuracy from those trails; each subject get 1 mean-score per task.

I was wondering whether blavaan, or blavaan in combination with something else, can estimate the manifest variables from the trial-level data instead of the aggregated means.

I hope I didn't over explain myself,

Jean-Paul

messages.author: 54c05e928c45ac6c
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical approach: estimating manifest variables from trial level data
parts:
Instead of declaring pCE, pNE, etc. as endogenous observed variables, declare them as latent variables. Next, specify those latent variables to each load onto 100 of a set of 3x100 = 300 endogenous observed indicators, where each indicator is one of the 300 accuracy indicators. You'll need to decide if the higher-level latent variables directly affect those measures, whether there are residual correlations between the measures, etc. just like in frequentist SEM. I imagine this will be a pain to fit both and require a ton of RAM.

I've mostly stayed away from blavaan for such cases due to the difficulty of parsing the underlying Stan code to understand/edit the model compared to writing my own Stan code, the difficulty of specifying informative priors without repeated prior predictive sampling due to its approach to ensuring covariance matrices are positive definite, and restrictions/ambiguity concerning hierarchical priors.

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical approach: estimating manifest variables from trial level data
parts:
One other thought: based on your path diagram, the 0/1 trial accuracies are independent Bernoullis conditioned on PER_E and PER_D. I think you could then model the number of trials correct (out of 100) as binomial with n=100, which would avoid large numbers of observed variables.

This isn't currently possible in blavaan, but it is probably the direction that I would go if I was coding the model manually.

Ed
